header.scope: Lost: international business moved to local acquiring after Adyen's test; the US stayed with us.
header.tag_why: Adyen tested a slice of his international traffic and returned results by country. We answered with an average uplift. Our own market-by-market analysis arrived three weeks after he asked, by which time the test was finished.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: For payments leaders who ask for their own numbers, lead with: Your approvals, market by market: by country, card type and issuer, with the reason for each decline pattern and the money left on the table. Use 'approvals' in the headline and keep 'authorization', Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance for the technical detail underneath. Do not lead with the average uplift.
messaging_changes.why: Stefan rejected the average outright ('that's an average. What's mine?'), defined proof as country, card type, issuer and why, and speaks of approvals and money left on the table rather than authorization and uplift.

messaging_changes.change: When a buyer is weighing a 'local acquiring' test, offer a per-country approvals diagnostic on their own traffic, with a committed delivery date that lands before the competitor's test ends. Suggested line: Before you decide, see your own approvals by country, card type and issuer, and why, from your own traffic. Confirm a realistic turnaround with the payments performance team before promising it, and only mention local routing where product confirms we offer it.
messaging_changes.why: Adyen won by testing his own traffic and reporting results by country, and our market-by-market analysis was the most useful thing we sent him but arrived three weeks after he asked, once the test had finished.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For payments owners, lead with a named person at Stripe who reviews your approvals every month, instead of response-time tiers. Suggested line: A named payments performance owner who looks at your numbers every month. Confirm with account management that we can staff this before using it.
messaging_changes.why: Stefan asked who at Stripe looks at his numbers every month and the rep had no name, he turned down the roadmap session, and he read our outreach as reactive ('I heard from Stripe when I said I was leaving.').

messaging_changes.change: Add a proof point the champion can take to the CFO: this customer's own approvals and the revenue at stake per market, set out in a short readout rather than a benchmark. Suggested framing: Here is the money left on the table in each of your markets, and what we would fix.
messaging_changes.why: The CFO approved Stefan's recommendation, and Stefan said plainly 'I can't take an average to my CFO.', so our proof had to work in a room we were never in.

trigger.insight: The evaluation started with a change of buyer, not a product failure. The person who bought us left last year, and nobody on our side met his replacement before the renewal. Stefan's first move was to look at declines by country, which is data we hold and could have shown him first. We still don't know which markets worried him, beyond a mention of Brazil and a couple in Europe.
trigger.messaging: When a new payments owner arrives at an account, open with an unprompted per-country approvals review of their own traffic, not the M1 'grow globally' line.

decider.insight: The CFO made the decision, and the transcript gives no sign that we ever reached the CFO. Stefan's job was to build a case the CFO would accept, and we gave him nothing he could carry into that room. By our last call the recommendation had already gone up two weeks earlier, so we were talking after the decision had left Stefan's hands.
decider.messaging: Make the approvals proof CFO-ready: show the customer's own revenue recovered per market, not a benchmark the champion can't present.

competitor.insight: Adyen won by running a test on his own traffic rather than by making a claim, and that reset what Stefan expected as proof: country, card type, issuer, and why. We don't know what the test actually showed. 'Local acquiring' became his frame, and our only reply was an ML-driven average. When the rep says she doesn't know what she'd have pitched, that misses the point: the counter was evidence, and we had it, but it came too late.
competitor.messaging: Against a local-acquiring test, offer a time-boxed, per-country approvals diagnostic on the customer's traffic within days, and say plainly where we already route locally (to be confirmed with product).

message.insight: The uplift number did not get silence; it got an explicit rejection. M4's average is what pushed him away. Stefan also turned down the roadmap session, and the one thing that landed was an analysis of his own data. The rep says 'we weren't really pitching' because it was a renewal, but we did present the Authorization Boost deck. The claim that 'developers love us' rests on the rep's read, not on anything the customer said.
message.messaging: Rewrite M4 so it leads with the customer's own approvals by market and issuer, with the reasons; drop the average uplift as the headline proof.

decided.insight: There were turning points, and they came before we were involved. We found out about the evaluation only when Stefan answered the renewal notice by asking to split the contract. Our analysis then took three weeks and arrived after the test was over. The rep's view that nothing could have been done doesn't hold up against her own statement that the analysis found things we could have fixed. The transcript does not show whether the analysis reached Stefan before or after the recommendation went to the CFO.
decided.messaging: Make it a renewal-motion rule that a per-market approvals review goes out before the renewal notice, not in reaction to a split request.

gaps.insight: The capability existed: our payments performance team produced the analysis he asked for. What was missing was speed and ownership. He wanted a named person reviewing his numbers every month, and we couldn't name one. The last business review took place before the current rep had the account, and the account was on nobody's watch list.
gaps.messaging: Make M5 a named payments-performance owner with a monthly approvals review, instead of a support plan described by response times.

language.insight: Stefan talks about approvals, money left on the table, and what's his. We talk about authorization, uplift, and Adaptive Acceptance. 'Local cards, local rails' was the frame Adyen's test gave him. His remark that he heard from Stripe when he said he was leaving shows he read our engagement as reactive retention, not as care for his account.
language.messaging: Rename the M4 headline in buyer terms ('your approvals, market by market: the money left on the table') and keep 'authorization' for the technical detail.

gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep for dates: Stefan's request, analysis delivery, test end, CFO submission. Did our analysis reach him before the recommendation went to the CFO?

gaps.question: Did anyone from our side ever meet the CFO?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the rep whether the CFO saw any Stripe material, and whether a CFO-level readout of our analysis is still possible to win back international.

close.rep_takeaway: Healthy, no tickets is not the same as safe. When the buyer who signed with us leaves, treat the account as up for grabs: meet the replacement and bring their own approval numbers before they go and find someone else to test them. When a buyer asks 'what's mine?', the fastest real answer from their own data beats any deck, and three weeks is too long.
